In this note we describe the natural coordinatizations of a Delzant space defined as a reduced phase space (symplectic geometry view-point) and give explicit formulas for the coordinate transformations. For each fixed point of the torus action on the Delzant polytope, we have a maximal coordinatization of an open cell in the Delzant space which contains the fixed point. This cell is equal to the domain of definition of one of the natural coordinatizations of the Delzant space as a toric variety (complex algebraic geometry view-point), and we give an explicit formula for the toric variety coordinates in terms of the reduced phase space coordinates. We use considerations in the maximal coordinate neighborhoods to give simple proofs of some of the basic facts about the Delzant space, as a reduced phase space, and as a toric variety. These can be viewed as a first application of the coordinatizations, and serve to make the presentation more self-contained.

Let \(\Delta\subset \mathfrak t^{*}\) be an \(n\)-dimensional Delzant polytope written as  
\[
\Delta=\{x\in\mathfrak t^{*}\mid \ell_j(x):=\langle x,u_j\rangle-\lambda_j\ge 0,\quad j=1,\ldots,d\},
\]
where the \(u_j\in\mathfrak t_{\mathbb Z}\) are the primitive inward-pointing normals to the facets. The Delzant condition says that exactly \(n\) facets meet at each vertex and that their normals form a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of the integral lattice. From these data one may construct the associated Delzant space in two standard ways: as a symplectic reduction of \(\mathbb C^d\), or as the smooth toric variety determined by the normal fan of \(\Delta\). Although the equivalence of the two constructions is classical, the coordinate charts arising naturally from them look quite different. The purpose of the note is to describe both families of maximal charts explicitly and to write down the transformation between them.

Define
\[
\beta:\mathbb R^d\longrightarrow \mathfrak t,\qquad \beta(e_j)=u_j,
\]
and let \(\mathfrak n=\ker\beta\). The corresponding subtorus \(N\subset T^d\) acts on \(\mathbb C^d\) by coordinatewise multiplication. With the constants \(\lambda_j\) incorporated into the standard moment map, reduction by \(N\) gives
\[
M_\Delta=J_N^{-1}(0)/N.
\]
The residual torus \(T^d/N\simeq T^n\) acts effectively and Hamiltonianly on \(M_\Delta\), with moment-map image equal to \(\Delta\). If a point of the reduced space has moment-map value \(x\), then it admits a representative \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\) satisfying
\[
\frac{|z_j|^2}{2}=\ell_j(x).
\]
Thus a coordinate vanishes exactly when the corresponding moment-map value lies on the associated facet.

Fix a vertex \(v\) of \(\Delta\), and let
\[
I_v=\{i_1,\ldots,i_n\}
\]
be the set of facets containing \(v\). Since the normals \(u_i\), \(i\in I_v\), form a lattice basis, every other normal has a unique expansion
\[
u_j=\sum_{i\in I_v}a_{ij}u_i,\qquad a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Consider the open subset
\[
U_v=\{[z]\in M_\Delta\mid z_j\neq 0\text{ for every }j\notin I_v\}.
\]
Its moment-map image is
\[
\Delta_v=\{x\in\Delta\mid \ell_j(x)>0\text{ for }j\notin I_v\},
\]
the complement in \(\Delta\) of the facets not containing \(v\). This is the largest natural invariant neighborhood of the fixed point corresponding to \(v\) on which all coordinates indexed by \(j\notin I_v\) remain nonzero.

The \(N\)-action can be used uniquely to choose a representative for which
\[
z_j>0\qquad(j\notin I_v).
\]
The remaining \(n\) complex coordinates,
\[
w_i=z_i,\qquad i\in I_v,
\]
then provide a symplectic-reduction chart. If \(\eta_i\in\mathfrak t^{*}\) denotes the basis dual to the normals at \(v\), so that
\[
\langle\eta_i,u_k\rangle=\delta_{ik},
\]
the corresponding moment-map value is
\[
x(w)=v+\frac12\sum_{i\in I_v}|w_i|^2\eta_i.
\]
The omitted coordinates are recovered from
\[
z_j=\sqrt{2\ell_j(x(w))},\qquad j\notin I_v.
\]
Consequently the domain of the chart is
\[
D_v=\{w\in\mathbb C^n\mid \ell_j(x(w))>0\text{ for all }j\notin I_v\}.
\]
This domain need not be all of \(\mathbb C^n\), but it is the maximal domain on which the above real gauge is available.

The toric-variety construction gives a second chart on the same neighborhood. Let \(N_{\mathbb C}\) be the complexification of \(N\). The toric variety may be presented as the appropriate quotient of the stable locus in \(\mathbb C^d\) by \(N_{\mathbb C}\). On the open set where \(z_j\neq0\) for \(j\notin I_v\), the complexified action can be used to normalize
\[
z_j=1,\qquad j\notin I_v.
\]
The coordinates that remain,
\[
\zeta_i,\qquad i\in I_v,
\]
identify this affine toric chart with \(\mathbb C^n\).

The relation between the two coordinate systems follows directly from the integral relations among the facet normals. For each \(j\notin I_v\), the vector
\[
e_j-\sum_{i\in I_v}a_{ij}e_i
\]
lies in \(\ker\beta\). Applying the corresponding element of \(N_{\mathbb C}\) to the real-gauge representative and normalizing the \(j\)-th coordinate to \(1\) gives
\[
\boxed{\;
\zeta_i
=
w_i\prod_{j\notin I_v}
\bigl(2\ell_j(x(w))\bigr)^{a_{ij}/2},
\qquad i\in I_v.
\;}
\]
All factors in this formula are positive on \(D_v\), so arbitrary integral exponents cause no ambiguity. This map is generally not holomorphic with respect to the standard complex structure in the \(w\)-variables: the \(w\)-coordinates are adapted to symplectic reduction, whereas the \(\zeta\)-coordinates are adapted to the algebraic torus action. Nevertheless, the formula defines a smooth equivariant diffeomorphism
\[
D_v\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n.
\]
Its inverse is obtained by solving the corresponding positive real equations for the moduli of the \(w_i\), while preserving their phases. Strict convexity of the associated toric potential, or an elementary monotonicity argument, gives existence and uniqueness.

This calculation also proves that the two apparently different open sets are the same. In the symplectic quotient, the chart consists of classes with \(z_j\neq0\) for \(j\notin I_v\). In the toric quotient, precisely the same nonvanishing condition permits normalization of those coordinates to \(1\). Thus the maximal symplectic cell and the affine toric cell attached to \(v\) coincide as subsets of the Delzant space; only their preferred coordinates differ.

These charts make several standard facts immediate. The origin in either coordinate system is the fixed point corresponding to \(v\), and every fixed point arises from a unique vertex. More generally, the pattern of vanishing coordinates records the face containing the moment-map value, yielding the usual inclusion-reversing correspondence between faces of \(\Delta\) and torus-orbit strata. Because the normals at every vertex form an integral basis, each local model is \(\mathbb C^n\), so the quotient is smooth rather than orbifold. The vertex cells cover the entire space, since every point of a compact polytope belongs to \(\Delta_v\) for at least one vertex \(v\). The local formulas also show directly that the residual torus action is effective and that the moment map has image exactly \(\Delta\).

From the toric viewpoint, the same cover proves that the complex quotient is a smooth toric variety, with affine charts indexed by the maximal cones of the normal fan. From the symplectic viewpoint, it provides explicit local coordinates on the reduced space without invoking a general slice theorem. The coordinate transformation above identifies the two smooth structures and exhibits concretely how the symplectic and algebraic constructions fit together. In this way, the maximal vertex charts supply simple, self-contained proofs of the fundamental local and global properties of Delzant spaces in both frameworks.

### Delzant’s Theorem

Delzant’s theorem is a central result in symplectic geometry. It establishes a correspondence between compact symplectic toric manifolds and certain convex polytopes, now known as Delzant polytopes. For a polytope to satisfy Delzant’s conditions, it must be simple, rational, and smooth.

This theorem allows complex geometric spaces to be studied through combinatorial objects. By examining a Delzant polytope, mathematicians can recover important information about the corresponding toric manifold, making the result valuable in geometry, topology, and mathematical physics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research-note introduction about Delzant spaces that compares their descriptions in symplectic geometry and complex algebraic geometry.
counterfactuals.output:
## Introduction

Delzant spaces occupy a natural meeting point between symplectic geometry and complex algebraic geometry. In symplectic terms, a Delzant space is a compact connected symplectic manifold \((M^{2n},\omega)\) equipped with an effective Hamiltonian action of an \(n\)-torus \(T^n\). A choice of moment map
\[
\mu:M\longrightarrow \mathfrak t^*
\]
produces a convex polytope \(\Delta=\mu(M)\). The Delzant classification theorem asserts that \(\Delta\) determines \((M,\omega,T^n)\), up to equivariant symplectomorphism, provided that \(\Delta\) is simple, rational, and smooth: exactly \(n\) facets meet at each vertex, and their primitive inward normals form a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of the integral lattice. Thus the global geometry of the Hamiltonian space is encoded by finite combinatorial data.

From the viewpoint of complex algebraic geometry, the same lattice data define a smooth complete toric variety. The normal fan \(\Sigma_\Delta\) of the polytope determines a variety \(X_{\Sigma_\Delta}\) containing the algebraic torus \((\mathbb C^\times)^n\) as a dense open orbit. Facets correspond to torus-invariant divisors, faces correspond to orbit closures, and the Delzant smoothness condition becomes the regularity condition on the cones of the fan. When \(\Delta\) is integral, it also determines an ample torus-equivariant line bundle, and its lattice points index monomial sections. In this polarized setting, the polytope records not only the underlying toric variety but also its projective embedding and Kähler class.

The two descriptions emphasize different constructions. Symplectic geometry realizes a Delzant space by Hamiltonian reduction, with the support constants of the facets controlling the symplectic form. Algebraic geometry constructs it by gluing affine toric charts associated with cones, or equivalently through a quotient in the sense of geometric invariant theory. These procedures are parallel manifestations of the same combinatorics: the exact sequence of lattices used in symplectic reduction reappears in the divisor and Cox-coordinate descriptions of the toric variety. Under a torus-invariant compatible complex structure, the symplectic manifold becomes biholomorphic to \(X_{\Sigma_\Delta}\), while \(\omega\) becomes a toric Kähler form whose moment image is \(\Delta\).

Some care is nevertheless required when passing between the two categories. A Delzant polytope need not be integral, so its symplectic form need not represent an integral cohomology class. The associated normal fan still determines a smooth projective toric variety, but the polytope defines an algebraic polarization only after the relevant integrality condition is imposed. Consequently, the fan primarily records the complex variety, whereas the placement and support numbers of the polytope record additional symplectic—or, in the integral case, polarized algebraic—data.

This note uses the Delzant polytope as a common language for these perspectives. Its aim is to compare moment-map and fan constructions, identify the correspondence between symplectic and algebraic invariants, and clarify which features belong to the underlying toric variety and which depend on the chosen symplectic form or polarization.

For a Delzant polytope  
\[
\Delta=\{x\in\mathfrak t^*:\ell_r(x)=\langle x,u_r\rangle-\lambda_r\ge 0,\ r=1,\dots,d\},
\]
the paper gives a concrete local description of the associated Delzant space \(M_\Delta\), obtained by symplectic reduction of \(\mathbb C^d\).

Its main results are:

- **Vertex-indexed coordinate charts.** For every vertex \(v\) of \(\Delta\), the facets meeting at \(v\) have primitive normals forming a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of the lattice. On the open subset where the coordinates corresponding to the other facets are nonzero, the quotient action has a unique gauge-fixed representative. The remaining \(n\) complex coordinates provide a chart on an open cell \(U_v\subset M_\Delta\).

- **Explicit chart domains and moment map.** If \(I_v\) is the set of facets through \(v\), the chart domain is described by the positivity of the remaining affine facet functions. In these coordinates, the moment-map point \(x\in\Delta\) is determined by
  \[
  \ell_i(x)=\tfrac12|z_i|^2,\qquad i\in I_v
  \]
  up to the paper’s normalization convention. Thus the geometry of each chart is read directly from the affine geometry of \(\Delta\).

- **Explicit transition maps.** On overlaps, the change of coordinates is expressed using the integral change-of-basis matrix between the normals at two vertices. Schematically, if
  \[
  u_k=\sum_{i\in I_v}a_{ki}u_i,
  \]
  then the \(k\)-th coordinate in the second chart has modulus determined by the facet function \(\ell_k(x)\) and phase
  \[
  \prod_{i\in I_v}\left(\frac{z_i}{|z_i|}\right)^{a_{ki}}.
  \]
  Hence
  \[
  z_k'=\sqrt{2\,\ell_k(x(z))}
  \prod_{i\in I_v}\left(\frac{z_i}{|z_i|}\right)^{a_{ki}},
  \]
  with harmless changes of constants depending on conventions. Integrality makes the formula single-valued, while apparent singularities disappear on the relevant overlap.

- **Basic properties proved from the atlas.** The charts establish directly that the quotient is a smooth Hausdorff \(2n\)-manifold, and that the reduced symplectic forms fit together smoothly. They also make transparent that the residual torus action is smooth, effective, and Hamiltonian, with moment-map image exactly \(\Delta\).

- **Orbit and boundary structure.** Vanishing chart coordinates correspond to lying on facets of \(\Delta\). More generally, stabilizers and orbit dimensions are determined by the face containing the moment-map value. Vertices correspond to torus fixed points, and the inverse image of the interior is the free, dense torus orbit region.

Overall, the paper turns the abstract reduction construction into an explicit atlas: the combinatorics and integral affine geometry of the Delzant polytope directly control the coordinates, transition functions, torus action, and local symplectic geometry of the resulting space.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please write a self-contained abstract for a note showing that each fixed point of a Delzant polytope determines a maximal coordinatization, identifying its domain with a natural toric-variety chart and deriving explicit formulas between the two coordinate systems.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(\Delta\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\) be a Delzant polytope and \(X_{\Delta}\) its associated smooth toric variety. We show that every vertex \(v\) of \(\Delta\), equivalently every torus fixed point \(p_v\in X_{\Delta}\), determines a canonical maximal coordinatization. If \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\in N\) are the primitive inward normals to the facets meeting at \(v\), the Delzant condition makes them a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(N\). Writing \(m_1,\ldots,m_n\in M\) for the dual basis, the resulting coordinates are the characters
\[
z_i=\chi^{m_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Their common domain is precisely the affine toric chart
\[
U_v=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma_v^\vee\cap M]\cong\mathbb C^n,
\]
where \(\sigma_v\) is the normal cone of \(\Delta\) at \(v\); the point \(p_v\) corresponds to the origin. We prove that this chart is maximal among torus-invariant coordinate neighborhoods adapted to \(p_v\). We also give explicit monomial changes of variables. Relative to a lattice basis and dense-torus coordinates \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), if \(m_i=(m_{i1},\ldots,m_{in})\) and \(u_i=(u_{i1},\ldots,u_{in})\), then
\[
z_i=\prod_{j=1}^{n}t_j^{m_{ij}},
\qquad
t_j=\prod_{i=1}^{n}z_i^{u_{ij}}.
\]
Thus the local coordinates arising from the fixed point agree exactly with the natural affine coordinates of the corresponding toric-variety chart, and transitions between vertex charts are integral Laurent monomials determined solely by the combinatorics of \(\Delta\).
